fixes.explanation: The nations far away aren't the ones Peter is talking to, friend. Peter is speaking to “Rulers and elders of the people!” (Acts 4:8) Then he says Jesus is “the stone you builders rejected…” (Acts 4:11) That “you” is aimed at the ones he's speaking to.

That's the one, friend. The text says the leaders were “…greatly disturbed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead.” (Acts 4:2) So the message was the trouble, and it brought the priests, the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees right up to Peter and John.

Nope, nothing in this passage says a word about offerings. The text says the leaders were disturbed that Peter and John were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead (Acts 4:2). So what disturbed them was the message, not money.
Five thousand, baker! The text says “…the number of men grew to about five thousand.” (Acts 4:4) It also says many who heard the message believed. That's a whole lot of believers, friend.

Moses, Israel's leader, doesn't come up in Peter's answer. Peter says it's “…by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth…” that the man stands there healed (Acts 4:10). Peter had one name on his lips, and it wasn't Moses.

Yes, baker. Peter is talking to “Rulers and elders of the people!” (Acts 4:8) and then says Jesus is “the stone you builders rejected…” (Acts 4:11) He says “you,” and the rulers and elders are the ones he's speaking to. Peter's not shy, that's for sure.

The temple isn't the word in this verse, friend. Peter says, “…there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.” (Acts 4:12) Salvation is tied to a name, and that name is Jesus.

Gamaliel was a Pharisee and a teacher of the law (Acts 5:34), but he's not the name in this verse. The council took note that Peter and John “…had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13) That's the name the verse gives.

True, friend. The text says that “…seeing the man who had been healed standing there with them, they had nothing to say in response.” (Acts 4:14) The healed man was right there with them. That's the kind of moment where you open your mouth and nothing comes out.
Traveling doesn't come up in their answer. They say, “For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.” (Acts 4:20) What they can't stop is speaking, not traveling.
It's the other way around, friend. The text says “…all the people were glorifying God for what had happened.” (Acts 4:21) That's why the council couldn't find a way to punish Peter and John.
Doubt isn't the word in this verse. The text says “…all the people were glorifying God for what had happened.” (Acts 4:21) A crowd that's praising God makes it hard for a council to punish anybody.

True, baker. The text says, “When the believers heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord.” (Acts 4:24) They lifted their voices together. The report came from Peter and John, who had returned to their own people (Acts 4:23).
The psalm doesn't say that. It says the kings and rulers gather together “…against the Lord and against His Anointed One.” (Acts 4:26) Those are the two it names, not a building or a city.

Boldness is right, baker. They pray, “…enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness…” (Acts 4:29) They'd just brought their council's threats before God, and they asked for complete boldness. I'd have asked for a different problem.

Judgment on their enemies isn't in the prayer. They say, “…consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness…” (Acts 4:29) What they ask is for God to enable them to speak His word with complete boldness.
Shaken, baker! The text says, “After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken…” (Acts 4:31) The place was shaken after the prayer. That's one memorable prayer meeting.

The text says the opposite, friend. After the shaking, “…they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.” (Acts 4:31) They spoke boldly, right after asking for exactly that.
